title: Follow a Network, Not Just One Boat
content:
The previous mission investigated boats and travel knowledge. Now ask how products could move through several communities. A network is a set of connected places or people. A product can pass through more than one trader before reaching its final user.

Read the classroom network diagram. It names China and the Philippines as modern geographical references, with an unnamed exchange stop between them. Step 1. Find where a product was made. Step 2. Follow the possible intermediate exchange. Step 3. Find where it was later used or deposited. The intermediate stop is fictional: the diagram illustrates indirect exchange, not a documented route for one particular object.

The National Museum reports Chinese, Vietnamese and Thai ceramics in Philippine collections, spanning different precolonial and colonial periods. That does not mean every type arrived at once. Studying the origin, date and find context is necessary before making a specific historical claim. A modern country name locates a region; it does not describe all past political borders.
clues: Origin is not the whole route
A vessel made in China could move through several exchanges. Its place of manufacture alone does not identify every trader or stop.
Chinese, Vietnamese and Thai examples in a collection are not evidence of one shipment or one century. Check each item rather than merging all dates.
The middle stop in this diagram is invented for teaching. Dashed links show a possible exchange pattern, not a record of an actual voyage.
task: A bowl made in China is found at a Philippine site. Which conclusion is careful?
It provides evidence for connections, but its exact route needs more sources
The maker certainly sailed directly to its final owner
Every similar bowl arrived in the same shipment
The manufacturing place identifies every person who used it
reason: A production origin and a find location support questions about connections. They do not by themselves prove a direct trip or every intermediate stop.
definition: Connected people and places through which goods can be exchanged.

title: Watch How: Read a Changsha Evidence Card
content:
Use a named example instead of just saying an imported bowl. The National Museum describes Changsha stoneware made in southern China and finds from Mt. Kamhantik in Mulanay, Quezon. Stoneware is a type of fired ceramic. The location and associated finds are part of its archaeological context.

Worked example: Step 1. Record the identified ceramic type and production region. Step 2. Record the Philippine find location and context. Step 3. State a limited conclusion: the material helps investigate connections beyond the archipelago. A description of the object does not identify its full travel history.

Compare with another source. The National Museum also describes Changsha bowls in the cargo of the Belitung shipwreck near Sumatra, in what is now Indonesia. That is evidence from a different site, not proof that the same ship visited Mulanay. Similar objects can connect research questions without turning two finds into one proven voyage.

The illustration is a source-summary card, not a photograph of an original object. Researchers compare materials, shapes, decorations and context rather than guessing from colour alone.
clues: Changsha stoneware refers to a ceramic production tradition associated with China. It is not the name of the Philippine find site.
Mt. Kamhantik and the Belitung wreck are different archaeological contexts. Their similar ceramic types do not prove a direct trip between them.
The examples help investigate wider maritime links. A claim naming a particular ship route needs additional evidence.
task: Similar Changsha ceramics occur at a Philippine site and a wreck near Sumatra. What should a report say?
Compare the separate contexts without claiming one proven voyage connects them
The same ship certainly deposited both finds
Both objects must have the same owner and date
Similar appearance makes the recorded find locations unnecessary
reason: Comparable ceramic types can inform research on connections. Separate contexts and dates must be checked before asserting a particular journey.
definition: The recorded setting and relationships of a find.

title: Field Journal: Connect Goods, People and Evidence
content:
Connect the discoveries from this mission. A network can include several stops. Ceramics have production histories and find contexts. Communities can exchange products to meet different needs while still farming, fishing and making things locally.

Return to the diagram. A dashed connection is an explanation to examine, not a photograph of every journey. A known production region and a find site do not reveal all the people between them. Compare objects with dated contexts and other sources before choosing a route claim.

Contact also creates opportunities to share knowledge and ideas. It does not make every community identical or mean local people had no knowledge of their own. Different groups can choose, adapt or retain practices.

Build a report with four parts: name the object or source, locate its context, explain what connection it supports, then state one limit. Save useful opened clues in your journal if you want to revisit them. The next mission looks more closely at goods, technologies and cultural exchange.
clues: Imported products could be valued for different reasons. Their presence does not mean communities stopped local production.
A route report becomes stronger when it compares sources and dates rather than drawing a line because two places have similar objects.
Knowledge and customs could be shared and adapted. Exchange does not prove complete cultural sameness.
task: Which final report best uses the mission evidence?
Goods and their contexts help investigate networks, while exact routes and shared practices need further support
One imported bowl records every journey and every belief
Trade means all communities stopped making local products
A fictional network stop is a documented ancient port
reason: The report connects evidence with a limited claim. Networks, needs and local choices matter without making one object a complete history.
definition: A statement whose explanation fits the available evidence.
